title: Sunny Deol and Akshaye Khanna Haven't Shared a Screen Since Border. Netflix Just Reunited Them — After 30 Years.
excerpt: Netflix India's 2026 Hindi slate is its most ambitious yet: a Kaththi remake with two double roles, a fifth Kapil Sharma season, a Kargil air-war drama, and Lust Stories 3. For the diaspora, all of it lands in one place, on day one.
body:
The last time Sunny Deol and Akshaye Khanna stood in the same frame, it was 1997, the film was Border, and an entire generation learned to cry at a J. P. Dutta war anthem. Twenty-nine years later, Netflix has done what no producer dared attempt: it has put them back together — and it's making the reunion the crown jewel of its biggest Hindi year ever.

Netflix India unveiled its 2026 slate this week, and it is, frankly, a flex. Nine original films, fifteen-plus series, and a strategy that reads less like a content calendar and more like a land grab. For the diaspora — the millions of us who keep a Netflix subscription precisely so we don't have to hunt for a sketchy stream the morning after a Mumbai premiere — it's the best kind of news. Everything here lands globally, in over 190 countries, on day one. No VPN. No waiting.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=LEargi83ofQ
The centerpiece is Ikka, and it is the kind of casting that makes you sit up.

Directed by Ali Abbas Zafar — the man who knows exactly how to weaponise a Sunny Deol entry — Ikka is the official Hindi remake of the Tamil blockbuster Kaththi. Deol is reportedly playing a double role, which means we get twice the dhai-kilo-ka-haath energy in a single film. Khanna, ever the silk-voiced antagonist, takes the high-stakes villain's chair. The two of them circling each other again, three decades after they shared the screen as brothers-in-arms, is the sort of nostalgia bomb that doesn't need a marketing budget. It sells itself.

But Zafar's actioner is just the headline. The slate underneath it is genuinely deep.

Taapsee Pannu returns in Gandhari, a Kanika Dhillon-produced revenge thriller directed by Devashish Makhija, billed as \"a revenge saga with a soul\" — Pannu as a mother on a mission, physical and feral, the kind of role she's spent a decade earning. Lust Stories 3 brings the fan-favourite anthology back for a third round of four-director, four-perspective urban intimacy — still the boldest mainstream franchise about how Indians actually love. And Accused, a legal thriller about a case that is never what it seems, rounds out a film lineup that swings from masala to murder.

The series side is where Netflix is really protecting its turf. The Great Indian Kapil Sharma Show returns for Season 5, with Kapil Sharma and Sunil Grover still doing the only thing that reliably cracks the Global Top 10 in a language most of the world doesn't speak. Ravi Kishan is back as VD Tyagi in Maamla Legal Hai Season 2, mining the gloriously absurd Patparganj District Court for more chaos. Bhuvan Bam expands the BB Ki Vines universe with Dhindora Season 2 at a visibly bigger budget. And Mismatched Season 4 sends Rohit Saraf and Prajakta Koli stumbling into adult life — the closest thing Indian streaming has to a comfort-watch coming-of-age.

The one that should make diaspora dads cancel their evening plans, though, is Operation Safed Sagar — a big-budget military drama chronicling the Indian Air Force's role in the Kargil War, complete with the kind of authentic aerial-combat sequences that Hindi cinema has historically faked with stock footage and prayer. If Netflix gets the dogfights right, this is appointment viewing in Edison, Hounslow and Brampton alike.

There's also Kohrra Season 2, the quietly devastating Punjabi-Hindi crime mystery that became a critics' darling; Glory, a new sports-crime thriller; and a clutch of fresh originals — Talaash: A Mother's Search, Family Business, Yeh Dil Sunn Raha Hai — that suggest Netflix is no longer just buying the obvious IP. It's building its own.

What's striking is the confidence of it. A few years ago the streaming-versus-theatre conversation in India was all hand-wringing. Now Netflix is announcing a slate this dense without a flicker of doubt about whether the audience will show up. They will. We will. Because for the diaspora, this was never really a choice between the big screen and the small one — the big screen is eleven time zones and a plane ticket away. Netflix is the screen we actually have.

The full 2026 rollout begins this year, with Ikka positioned as the marquee launch. Mark it. A Border reunion doesn't come around twice.
